summary: Repository-mining study using a staggered difference-in-differences design (Sun and Abraham estimator) on 2,808 GitHub repos with more than 100 stars. Adoption is dated by each repo's first agent-authored PR in the AIDev dataset; the repos are compared with 8,289 propensity-matched controls from GHArchive over January 2023 to May 2026. It reports no change in the number of human PR authors, a 1.9-point drop in human PR authors per PR, a 3.7-point drop in the newcomer share of human PR authors, and 5.3% more review comments per review event. All outcomes are PR-event proxies. The proposed mechanism ('dilution' rather than newcomer displacement) is not identified by the design and is contradicted by the paper's own numbers.

claims.claim: AI agent adoption does not change the absolute number of human contributors (ATT 0.014, p=0.224)
claims.evidence: §IV-A, Fig. 1: aggregate ATT not significant. However, the pre-treatment coefficients drift from about -0.30 at month -12 toward zero; the authors themselves say parallel trends are partially violated and demote this outcome to a robustness check.

claims.claim: Human contributor density falls by 1.9 points (ATT -0.019, p=0.002), so the human share of participation declines
claims.evidence: §IV-A, Fig. 2: pre-trends are flat. Density is human PR authors divided by all PRs. Codex, Claude Code and Cursor PRs are opened from human accounts, so the metric largely tracks PRs per human, and §VI concedes the effect is 'partly mechanical'. The paper is also inconsistent with itself: Table III shows treated density rising from 0.476 to 0.577 even though the text calls the direction 'consistent'; the event study reaches about -0.13 at month 12 while the aggregate ATT is -0.019; and §IV-D calls the full-sample p=0.002 result 'marginal'.

claims.claim: Newcomers' relative participation share drops 3.7 points (about 10.6%), immediately after adoption and stably
claims.evidence: §IV-B, Fig. 3/4: pre-trends are flat for the ratio. The body reports p=0.001 while the abstract says p<0.001 (SE 0.007 implies p<0.001, so this looks like a typo). Adoption dates come from the AIDev collection window (1,054 repos 'adopt' in June 2025, which coincides with the Codex and Copilot agent launches). Control repos may have adopted agents that AIDev did not see. Java subgroup: ATT -0.067, p=0.107, not significant.

claims.claim: Review depth rises 5.3%, so agents shift burden from code production to review
claims.evidence: §IV-C, Fig. 5: ATT +0.0168 on review comments per review event. The metric is defined only for repo-months with any review, which excludes 58.9% of the panel. It does not measure review time, total review load, or reviewer count. The effect is not significant in any of the six language subgroups (Table V). The 'burden shift' interpretation goes beyond what the metric measures.

claims.claim: The newcomer decline is consistent with dilution (denominator growth) rather than displacement of newcomer tasks
claims.evidence: §V argues the decline is consistent with AI PRs growing the denominator, but the newcomer ratio's denominator is human contributors, not PRs. RQ1 finds that denominator unchanged, and the log newcomer count also falls (ATT -0.044, p<0.001, though its pre-trends are violated). The paper's own numbers therefore point to fewer newcomers, which is the displacement reading it sets aside.

patterns.note: Evidence on the risk that motivates P41: after adoption, newcomers make up a smaller share of human PR authors (ATT -0.037), and the authors suggest agents occupy the starter tasks newcomers learn on. No comprehension measure, and no safeguard (walkthroughs, reserved starter tasks) is tested. The mechanism is not identified.
Human review comments per review rise 5.3% after adoption. No gate design is compared, and total review burden is not measured.
Observational field data from 11,097 OSS repos. This is field evidence about agent adoption, not a test of whether field evaluation is a better practice.

methodology.sample: 2,808 treated repos (>100 stars, in AIDev) plus 8,289 propensity-matched controls; 41 monthly periods; 454,977 repo-months
methodology.baselines: 1:3 nearest-neighbour propensity matching on six activity covariates, three of which have SMD 0.119-0.132 (above the 0.10 threshold); never-treated controls
methodology.models: Five agents pooled (Copilot, Codex, Cursor, Devin, Claude Code); no per-agent results
methodology.variance: Repo-clustered SEs; 95% CIs in event-study plots
methodology.ablations: Median-split moderators (stars, maturity) and six per-language subsamples; alternative count outcomes
methodology.contamination_controls: n/a. Bot filtering is a login substring match on 'bot' plus three named accounts; agent accounts such as 'Copilot' would not match and are not discussed
methodology.languages: Mostly TypeScript, Python, Rust; Java subsample of 646 repos shows no significant effect

standards.artifacts: Uses public GHArchive and AIDev data, but the replication package reference is an anonymised placeholder ('A. Author (2026)') with no resolvable link in the text

biases.detail: 'Human contributor density' counts PRs opened from human accounts (including agent-assisted ones) and mostly tracks PRs per author. 'Review depth' is comments per review event, which is not review burden.
Adoption is the first PR AIDev observed, and AIDev's collection window clusters adoption in May-July 2025. Control repos are 'not in AIDev', not verified non-adopters.
28 treated repos with no human PRs were dropped after a manual look at a 'representative subset'. About 260 repos were deleted or private at collection time.
The replication package citation is a placeholder, so availability cannot be verified.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Five commercial coding agents, pooled; none favoured

verdict_reason: The design (staggered DiD with Sun and Abraham, pre-trend checks, a large panel) is sound, and the newcomer-share effect survives its own pre-trend test. The headline interpretation does not hold up: the density and review-depth constructs are PR-event proxies, the descriptive and aggregate numbers disagree with the text in several places, and the 'dilution, not displacement' mechanism is contradicted by the paper's own outcome definitions. Cite the newcomer-share ATT only, as an OSS association.
applicability: Indirect. These are OSS newcomers measured as PR authors, not new employees on a Java backend team, and the Java subgroup is not significant. The transferable point is a risk, not a remedy: if agents take the small, well-scoped tickets new developers normally learn the repositories on, the onboarding path shrinks. The harness could reserve some starter tickets for humans, or require an agent-produced walkthrough that the new developer explains back before merge (P41), and track review load directly (time and reviewer count) rather than citing this paper's +5.3%.

conflicts_with.detail: Monperrus argues human code review (including its knowledge-transfer role) can be replaced by agents. This paper reports human review comments per review rising after agent adoption. The metric is weak, but the direction runs against the 'end of review' position.
